title: Wildernesses of the heart
hookLine: five barren places in the heart: doubt about teacher, teaching, community, training, and anger at companions (MN 16)
last: PLEASURE — THE ESCAPE IS FROM THE HOOK.

cards: A farmer can buy the best seed in the world, and if the field is full of stones and old stumps, not much comes up. Before planting, you clear the ground. It's slow, heavy work, with nothing to show for it yet.
The Buddha described five patches of barren, stony ground in the heart, and five things that tie it down, and said the practice won't grow until they're dealt with.

teach.b: MN 16, the Cetokhila. Ceto means heart or mind. Khila is harder to pin down: translators render it barrenness, wasteland, or a stake, something hard and stiff driven into the ground.
Either way, it's ground that won't take seed. The five are doubt about the Teacher, the teaching, the community, and the training.
And the fifth: anger at your companions in the practice, being displeased and resentful toward them. That last one isn't about doctrine at all.
Irritation with the people you practice alongside can make the ground as barren as any doubt.

Then five shackles that bind the heart: desire for sense pleasures, attachment to the body, attachment to outward forms, eating your fill and then indulging in sleep and lying around, and living the spiritual life only to be reborn among the gods.
And a picture for the cleared field.
A hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs. She sits on them, keeps them warm, turns them properly.
Even if no wish arises in her, may my chicks break out safely with their claws and beaks, they'll hatch anyway.

In the sutta, the hen's patient work stands for fifteen things: the five wildernesses cleared, the five shackles cut, four bases of spiritual power developed, and enthusiasm. The eggs are warmed, not forced.

how: Buddhist communities often encourage practitioners to bring doubts to a teacher rather than leave them unspoken, and the monastic rule sets out procedures for settling disputes between members.

o: a heavy stone used to grind grain
a fence built around a sacred grove
a barren, stony place in the heart

p: warms her eggs; they hatch anyway

s: all five wildernesses are kinds of doubt
four are doubts; the fifth is anger at your companions.
the hen has to wish for her chicks to hatch
even with no wish, eggs brooded properly hatch.
one shackle is practicing only to be reborn among the gods
the fifth of the five shackles.

games.q: a hen has twelve eggs. what does the simile say she has to do for them to hatch?
o: wish hard for her chicks every day
sit on them, keep them warm, turn them properly
games.why: she just does the patient work. the chicks hatch whether or not she wishes for it.

practice: Look over the field honestly: is there a doubt that's gone hard and stony, about a teacher, a practice, a community you belong to? Or is it the fifth one, irritation with someone who shares your path?
Pick one patch and just loosen it a little, breathing with it the way a hen sits warmly on her eggs.

wordCard.voice: Cetokhila, barrenness of the heart. Five barren places, four doubts and anger at your companions, cleared so the practice can grow.

orig.note: Pali cetokhila: wilderness, barrenness or stake of the heart; the name of MN 16.

carryVoice: Your line: clear the field. Patient work, and the eggs hatch in their time. See you tomorrow.
